To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MAFA is a key regulator of beta cell-specific genes involved in insulin biosynthesis, secretion and metabolism–secretion-coupling.
MAFA is a transcription factor that is expressed in beta cells and that controls the production of several important genes that are required for beta cell function.
MAFA controls genes implicated not only in insulin transcription, but more broadly in insulin biosynthesis, processing, secretion and signalling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the transcriptional regulation of insulin biosynthesis and release.
the transcriptional control of genes that are important for the maintenance of beta cell function and survival.
the identification and characterisation of a novel beta cell transcriptional master switch.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MAFA is an essential transcription factor for beta-cell function.
MAFA is a key regulator of beta-cell gene expression and function and that it is involved in the development of type 2 diabetes.
the MAFA gene product is the master regulator of beta cell-specific gene expression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MAFA is the key transcriptional regulator of beta-cell function and survival.
MAFA is a key transcription factor for beta-cell-specific insulin gene expression and for beta-cell identity.
MAFA is a master regulator of the insulin gene and other genes that are important for the function of beta cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MAFA is a master regulator of insulin production and beta cell function, and that MAFA may be a target for the treatment of diabetes.
MAFA is a master regulator of the beta cell phenotype.

MAFA is the most potent activator of insulin gene expression and that its overproduction in INS-1 cells leads to a marked increase in the number of insulin granules, which in turn enhances glucose-stimulated insulin release.
